newsitem.title: USA: Seagram wins USA Networks battle agianst Viacom.
newsitem.headline: Seagram wins USA Networks battle agianst Viacom.

text.p: Seagram Co Ltd said it won a significant victory Thursday in its legal battle against Viacom Inc related to their jointly owned USA Networks cable television partnership.
Seagram attorney Michael Schwartz told Reuters that Vice Chancellor Myron Steele of the Delaware Chancery Court had ruled in Seagram's favor.
"He said they breached the contract," Schwartz said. "Steele said Viacom's counter claims were 'specious.' But he left time for us to work things out."

In a 55-page opinion, Steele said, "The evidence is overwhelming that Viacom's current holdings consist of national video advertiser supported basic cable networks -- a direct conflict with the non-compete provisions of the USA agreement."

But Steele went on to say: "I conclude that when the parties' agreements have been breached but neither the innocent party nor the venture suffers immediate quantifiable harm, the equitable powers of this court afford me broad discretion in fashioning appropriate relief."

Seagram claimed during a trial last year that a Viacom violation of the USA Networks partnership agreement would trigger a buy/sell mechanism that would allow Seagram either to sell its partnership stake at the high end of a price valuation range, or buy out Viacom's half at the lower end.
But, in his opinion, Steele ordered both sides to work out a plan for discontinuing the USA Networks partnership in its present form, taking into account his legal and factual conclusions.
"The plan should provide for disposing of the assets used in the (partnership)... and be submitted within 30 days," Steele said.
Steele said that until a plan is submitted he will take no action on Seagram's requests for an injunction against Viacom's breach of the noncompete clause.

Seagram has maintained that Viacom's ownership and operation of the MTV and Nickelodeon Nick at Nite TV Land networks violated the terms of the 1981 joint partnership agreement entered into by Seagram subsidiary MCA Inc and Viacom subsidiary Paramount Communications Inc.
In negotiations that temporarily halted the trial in October, Viacom reportedly agreed to buy out Seagram for $1.7 billion.
Later, Seagram Chief Edgar Bronfman Jr. testified the deal fell through because he balked at paying the related high tax bill.
